questions.question: Three masses \(m_{1} = 4\) kg, \(m_{2} = 4\) kg and \(m_{3} = 6\) kg are suspended from a fixed smooth frictionless pulley as shown in the figure below. The value of \(T_{1} / T_{2}\) is _____. (take \(g = 10\) m/s\(^{2}\))
questions.explanation:
### Step 1: Draw the Free Body Diagram and write equations of motion

Given masses are \(m_{1} = 4\) kg, \(m_{2} = 4\) kg, and \(m_{3} = 6\) kg. Take \(g = 10\) m/s\(^{2}\).
From the Free Body Diagram, assuming \(m_{1}\) moves upwards with acceleration \(a\) and \(m_{2}\) and \(m_{3}\) move downwards with the same acceleration \(a\):
• For mass \(m_{1}\): \(T_{1} - m_{1}g = m_{1}a \Rightarrow T_{1} - 4 \times 10 = 4a \Rightarrow T_{1} - 40 = 4a\) (Equation 1)
• For mass \(m_{2}\): \(m_{2}g + T_{2} - T_{1} = m_{2}a \Rightarrow 4 \times 10 + T_{2} - T_{1} = 4a \Rightarrow 40 + T_{2} - T_{1} = 4a\) (Equation 2)
• For mass \(m_{3}\): \(m_{3}g - T_{2} = m_{3}a \Rightarrow 6 \times 10 - T_{2} = 6a \Rightarrow 60 - T_{2} = 6a\) (Equation 3)

### Step 2: Solve the system of equations for acceleration \(a\)

Add Equation 1, Equation 2, and Equation 3:
(T_{1} - 40) + (40 + T_{2} - T_{1}) + (60 - T_{2}) = 4a + 4a + 6a
T_{1} - 40 + 40 + T_{2} - T_{1} + 60 - T_{2} = 14a
60 = 14a
a = \frac{60}{14} = \frac{30}{7} \text{ m/s}^2

### Step 3: Calculate \(T_{1}\) and \(T_{2}\)

From Equation 1:
T_{1} = 40 + 4a = 40 + 4 \times \frac{30}{7}
T_{1} = 40 + \frac{120}{7} = \frac{280 + 120}{7} = \frac{400}{7} \text{ N}
From Equation 3:
T_{2} = 60 - 6a = 60 - 6 \times \frac{30}{7}
T_{2} = 60 - \frac{180}{7} = \frac{420 - 180}{7} = \frac{240}{7} \text{ N}

### Step 4: Calculate the ratio \(T_{1} / T_{2}\)

\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}} = \frac{400/7}{240/7} = \frac{400}{240}
\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}} = \frac{40}{24} = \frac{5}{3}
The value of \(T_{1} / T_{2}\) is \(5/3\).

questions.question: A car is moving on a horizontal curved road with radius 50 m. The approximate maximum speed of car will be, if friction between tyres and road is 0.34. [take \(g = 10 \text{ ms}^{-2}\)]

The rain drop of mass 1 g, starts with zero velocity from a height of 1 km. It hits the ground with a speed of 5 m/s. The work done by the unknown resistive force is _________ J. (take \(g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2\))
questions.explanation:
### Step 1: Apply the Work-Energy Theorem

According to the Work-Energy Theorem, the total work done on an object is equal to the change in its kinetic energy.
W_{\text{total}} = \Delta K
The total work done includes the work done by gravity (\(W_g\)) and the work done by the resistive force (\(W_{\text{res}}\)).
W_g + W_{\text{res}} = \Delta K

### Step 2: Express work done by gravity and change in kinetic energy

The work done by gravity when the rain drop falls from height \(h\) is \(mgh\). The change in kinetic energy is \(\frac{1}{2}mv^2 - \frac{1}{2}mu^2\). Since the rain drop starts with zero velocity, \(u=0\).
mgh + W_{\text{res}} = \frac{1}{2}mv^2

### Step 3: Isolate the work done by the resistive force

W_{\text{res}} = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - mgh

### Step 4: Substitute the given values and calculate

Given values:
• Mass \(m = 1 \text{ g} = 1 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg}\)
• Height \(h = 1 \text{ km} = 1000 \text{ m}\)
• Final velocity \(v = 5 \text{ m/s}\)
• Acceleration due to gravity \(g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2\)
W_{\text{res}} = \frac{1}{2}(1 \times 10^{-3})(5)^2 - (1 \times 10^{-3})(10)(1000)
W_{\text{res}} = \frac{1}{2}(1 \times 10^{-3})(25) - (1 \times 10^{-3})(10000)
W_{\text{res}} = 10^{-3} \left( \frac{25}{2} - 10000 \right)
W_{\text{res}} = 10^{-3} (12.5 - 10000)
W_{\text{res}} = 10^{-3} (-9987.5)
W_{\text{res}} = -9.9875 \text{ J}
Rounding to two decimal places, the work done by the resistive force is \(-9.98 \text{ J}\).

A block of \(\sqrt{3}\) kg is attached to a string whose other end is attached to the wall. An unknown force F is applied so that the string makes an angle of \(30^\circ\) with the wall. The tension T is: (Given \(g = 10 \text{ ms}^{-2}\))
questions.explanation:
### Step 1: Draw the Free Body Diagram and resolve forces

From the free body diagram, for equilibrium, the sum of forces in the horizontal and vertical directions must be zero.

### Step 2: Apply equilibrium conditions

Balancing forces in the horizontal direction:
F = T\sin 30^\circ
Balancing forces in the vertical direction:
\sqrt{3}g = T\cos 30^\circ

### Step 3: Solve for F and T

Divide the first equation by the second equation:
\frac{F}{\sqrt{3}g} = \frac{T\sin 30^\circ}{T\cos 30^\circ} = \tan 30^\circ
\frac{F}{\sqrt{3}g} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}
Given \(g = 10 \text{ ms}^{-2}\), we can find F:
F = g = 10 \text{ N}
Now, substitute F into the equation \(F = T\sin 30^\circ\):
10 = T \times \frac{1}{2}
T = 10 \times 2 = 20 \text{ N}
The tension T is 20 N.

questions.question: A body of mass 10 kg is moving with an initial speed of 20 m/s. The body stops after 5 s due to friction between body and the floor. The value of the coefficient of friction is: (Take acceleration due to gravity \(g = 10 \text{ ms}^{-2}\))
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution


### Step 1: Identify given values and relevant equations

Given:
• Initial speed \(u = 20 \text{ m/s}\)
• Final speed \(v = 0 \text{ m/s}\) (body stops)
• Time \(t = 5 \text{ s}\)
• Acceleration due to gravity \(g = 10 \text{ ms}^{-2}\)
We use the first equation of motion:
v = u + at

### Step 2: Calculate the acceleration

Substitute the given values into the equation of motion:
0 = 20 + a(5)
5a = -20
a = -4 \text{ ms}^{-2}
The negative sign indicates that the acceleration is in the opposite direction to the motion, which is due to friction.

### Step 3: Relate acceleration to the coefficient of friction

The force of friction \(f = \mu N\), where \(\mu\) is the coefficient of friction and \(N\) is the normal force. For a body on a horizontal surface, \(N = mg\).
According to Newton's second law, \(F = ma\). Here, the frictional force is the only force causing the deceleration:
ma = \mu mg
From this, we can find the acceleration due to friction:
a = \mu g

### Step 4: Calculate the coefficient of friction

Using the magnitude of acceleration calculated in Step 2:
4 = \mu (10)
\mu = \frac{4}{10}
\mu = 0.4

questions.explanation:
### Step 1: Identify forces and set up Free Body Diagram (FBD)

The forces acting on the garden roller are its weight \(Mg\) acting downwards, the normal reaction \(N\) from the ground acting upwards, and the applied force \(\vec{F}\) of \(200 \text{ N}\) acting at \(30^{\circ}\) below the horizontal. There is also a frictional force \(f\) opposing motion, but it does not affect the normal reaction in the vertical direction.

### Step 2: Resolve forces in vertical direction

Since the roller is in equilibrium (not accelerating vertically), the net force in the vertical direction must be zero. The vertical component of the applied force \(\vec{F}\) is \(F\sin30^{\circ}\) acting downwards, as the force is pushed at \(30^{\circ}\) below the horizontal.
\sum F_y = 0

N = Mg + F\sin30^{\circ}

### Step 3: Substitute values and calculate normal reaction

N = 700 + 200 \sin30^{\circ}
Using the value \(\sin30^{\circ} = 0.5\),
N = 700 + 200 \times 0.5
N = 700 + 100
N = 800 N

### Detailed Solution

The tension in the spring provides the necessary centripetal force for the circular motion. If \(x\) is the extension in the spring, then the radius of the circular path is \(r = l + x\). The tension in the spring is \(T = kx\).

kx = m\omega^2 (l+x)

### Step 2: Substitute values and solve for extension \(x\)

7.5x = 0.1 \times (5)^2 \times (0.2 + x)
7.5x = 0.1 \times 25 \times (0.2 + x)

5x = 0.5
x = \frac{0.5}{5} = 0.1\text{ m}

### Step 3: Calculate the tension in the spring

Now, the tension in the spring is given by \(T = kx\).
T = 7.5 \times 0.1\text{ N}
T = 0.75\text{ N}
The tension in the spring is 0.75 N.

A particle of mass m is initially at rest at the origin. It is subjected to a force and starts moving along the x-axis. Its kinetic energy K changes with time as \(dK/dt = \gamma t\) where \(\gamma\) is a positive constant of appropriate dimensions. Which of the following statements is (are) true?
options: The force applied on the particle is constant
The speed of the particle is proportional to time
The distance of the particle from the origin increases linearly with time
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

Given that the particle is initially at rest at the origin, and its kinetic energy K changes with time as \(dK/dt = \gamma t\).
We know that kinetic energy \(K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\).
Also, the rate of change of kinetic energy is equal to the power delivered by the force, which is \(P = Fv = \frac{dK}{dt}\).
We also know that \(F = m\frac{dv}{dt}\).
So, \(m\frac{dv}{dt} v = \frac{dK}{dt}\).
mv \frac{dv}{dt} = \gamma t
v dv = \frac{\gamma}{m} t dt
Integrating both sides:
\int v dv = \int \frac{\gamma}{m} t dt
\frac{v^2}{2} = \frac{\gamma}{m} \frac{t^2}{2} + C
Since the particle starts from rest at the origin, at \(t=0\), \(v=0\). Thus, the integration constant \(C=0\).
\frac{v^2}{2} = \frac{\gamma}{m} \frac{t^2}{2}
v^2 = \frac{\gamma}{m} t^2
v = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{m}} t
This implies that \(v \propto t\). So, statement (B) is TRUE.
Now, let's find the acceleration \(a = \frac{dv}{dt}\).
\frac{dv}{dt} = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{m}}
Since \(\sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{m}}\) is a constant, the acceleration is constant.
The force applied on the particle is \(F = m\frac{dv}{dt} = m \sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{m}} = \sqrt{m\gamma}\).
Since \(m\) and \(\gamma\) are constants, \(F\) is constant. So, statement (A) is TRUE.
A force is conservative if it can be expressed as the negative gradient of a scalar potential energy function. For a force that is constant and acts along the x-axis, it is a conservative force. So, statement (D) is TRUE.
Now, let's find the position \(x\). We know \(v = \frac{dx}{dt}\).
\frac{dx}{dt} = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{m}} t
dx = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{m}} t dt
Integrating both sides:
\int dx = \int \sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{m}} t dt
x = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{m}} \frac{t^2}{2} + C'
Since the particle starts from the origin, at \(t=0\), \(x=0\). Thus, the integration constant \(C'=0\).
x = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{m}} t^2
This implies that \(x \propto t^2\). Therefore, the distance of the particle from the origin increases quadratically with time, not linearly. So, statement (C) is FALSE.
Thus, the true statements are (A), (B), and (D).

questions.question: A student skates up a ramp that makes an angle \(30^\circ\) with the horizontal. He/she starts (as shown in the figure) at the bottom of the ramp with speed \(v_0\) and wants to turn around over a semicircular path xyz of radius \(R\) during which he/she reaches a maximum height \(h\) (at point y) from the ground as shown in the figure. Assume that the energy loss is negligible and the force required for this turn at the highest point is provided by his/her weight only. Then (g is the acceleration due to gravity)
options: the centripetal force required at points x and z is zero
the centripetal force required is maximum at points x and z
questions.explanation:
### Energy Conservation at Point Y

By the energy conservation (ME) between the bottom point and point Y:
\frac{1}{2}mv_0^2 = mgh + \frac{1}{2}mv_1^2
Rearranging this equation, we get the velocity at point Y, \(v_1\):
v_1^2 = v_0^2 - 2gh \quad \text{... (i)}

### Centripetal Force at Point Y

At point Y, the centripetal force is provided by the component of \(mg\) along the radius. From the diagram, the angle of the ramp with the horizontal is \(30^\circ\). The component of \(mg\) perpendicular to the ramp (and thus along the radius of the circular path at point Y) is \(mg \sin 30^\circ\).
mg \sin 30^\circ = \frac{mv_1^2}{R}
Since \(\sin 30^\circ = \frac{1}{2}\), we can simplify this to find \(v_1^2\):
v_1^2 = \frac{gR}{2}

### Combining Equations

Substitute the expression for \(v_1^2\) from the centripetal force equation into equation (i):
\frac{gR}{2} = v_0^2 - 2gh
This matches option (A).

### Centripetal Force at Points X and Z

At points x and z of the circular path, the points are at the same height, but this height is less than \(h\) (the height of point y). Due to energy conservation, if the height is less, the velocity will be greater than the velocity at point y.
The centripetal force is given by \(F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r}\). Since the velocity \(v\) at points x and z is greater than at point y, and the radius \(r\) is the same, the required centripetal force will be maximum at points x and z (where the velocity is highest in the circular path segment).
Therefore, option (D) is also correct.
Final Answer: A, D

A particle of mass m is moving in the xy-plane such that its velocity at a point \((x, y)\) is given as \(\vec{v} = \alpha(y\hat{x} + 2x\hat{y})\), where \(\alpha\) is a non-zero constant. What is the force \(\vec{F}\) acting on the particle ?
questions.explanation:
Given velocity vector:
\vec{v} = \alpha(y\hat{x} + 2x\hat{y})
From this, the components of velocity are:
v_x = \alpha y
v_y = 2\alpha x
Now, we find the components of acceleration by differentiating with respect to time:
a_x = \frac{dv_x}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}(\alpha y) = \alpha \frac{dy}{dt} = \alpha v_y
Substitute \(v_y = 2\alpha x\) into the expression for \(a_x\):
a_x = \alpha (2\alpha x) = 2\alpha^2 x
a_y = \frac{dv_y}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}(2\alpha x) = 2\alpha \frac{dx}{dt} = 2\alpha v_x
Substitute \(v_x = \alpha y\) into the expression for \(a_y\):
a_y = 2\alpha (\alpha y) = 2\alpha^2 y
So, the acceleration vector is:
\vec{a} = a_x \hat{x} + a_y \hat{y} = 2\alpha^2 x \hat{x} + 2\alpha^2 y \hat{y} = 2\alpha^2 (x\hat{x} + y\hat{y})
According to Newton's second law, the force acting on the particle is \(\vec{F} = m\vec{a}\):
\vec{F} = m [2\alpha^2 (x\hat{x} + y\hat{y})] = 2m\alpha^2 (x\hat{x} + y\hat{y})

questions.question: The CORRECT statement(s) for cubic close packed (ccp) three dimensional structure is (are) :
options: The number of the nearest neighbours of an atom present in the topmost layer is 12
The efficiency of an atom packing is 74%
The number of octahedral and tetrahedral voids per atom are 1 and 2, respectively
The unit cell edge length is $$2 \sqrt 2$$ times the radius of the atom
questions.explanation:
Coordination number cannot be 12, for any atom in the topmost layer, as there is no layer above it. Thus, each atom is in contact with six atoms in the same layer and three atoms from the layer below it.
For cubic close packing, we have
Packing fraction = $${{Volume\,of\,four\,spheres\,in\,the\,unit\,cell} \over {Total\,volume\,of\,the\,unit\,cell}}$$
$$ = 4 \times {{(4/3)\pi {r^3}} \over {16\sqrt 2 {r^3}}} = {\pi  \over {3\sqrt 2 }} = 0.74 = 74\% $$
In fcc unit cell, the effective number of atoms is
One atom at each corner = 8 corner atoms $$ \times {1 \over 8} = 1$$
Atoms at each of the six face centres :
6 face centered atoms $$ \times {1 \over 2} = 3$$.
Number of octahedral voids = 4.
Number of tetrahedral voids = 8.
Therefore, per atom, there is one octahedral void and two tetrahedral voids.
In fcc (or ccp), the unit edge length is given by
$$\sqrt 2 a = 4r \Rightarrow a = {{4r} \over {\sqrt 2 }} = 2\sqrt 2 r$$

A particle is moved along a path AB-BC-CD-DE-EF-FA, as shown in figure, in presence of a force \(\vec{F} = (\alpha y \hat{i} + 2\alpha x \hat{j})\) N, where x and y are in meter and \(\alpha = -1\) N/m\(^{-1}\). The work done on the particle by this force \(\vec{F}\) will be ______ Joule.
questions.explanation:
Given force \(\vec{F} = (\alpha y \hat{i} + 2\alpha x \hat{j})\). Since \(\alpha = -1\) N/m\(^{-1}\), the force is \(\vec{F} = (-y \hat{i} - 2x \hat{j})\).
W_{AB} = (-1\hat{i}) \cdot (1\hat{i}) = -1J
For path AB, \(y=1\) and \(d\vec{r} = dx \hat{i}\). \(\vec{F} = (-1\hat{i} - 2x\hat{j})\). \(W_{AB} = \int_{0}^{1} (-1) dx = -1\) J.
Similarly,
W_{BC} = 1J
For path BC, \(x=1\) and \(d\vec{r} = dy \hat{j}\). \(\vec{F} = (-y\hat{i} - 2\hat{j})\). \(W_{BC} = \int_{1}^{0.5} (-2) dy = [-2y]_{1}^{0.5} = -1 - (-2) = 1\) J.
W_{CD} = 0.25J
For path CD, \(y=0.5\) and \(d\vec{r} = dx \hat{i}\). \(\vec{F} = (-0.5\hat{i} - 2x\hat{j})\). \(W_{CD} = \int_{1}^{0.5} (-0.5) dx = [-0.5x]_{1}^{0.5} = -0.25 - (-0.5) = 0.25\) J.
W_{DE} = 0.5 J
For path DE, \(x=0.5\) and \(d\vec{r} = dy \hat{j}\). \(\vec{F} = (-y\hat{i} - 1\hat{j})\). \(W_{DE} = \int_{0.5}^{0} (-1) dy = [-y]_{0.5}^{0} = 0 - (-0.5) = 0.5\) J.
W_{EF} = W_{FA} = 0 J
For path EF, \(y=0\) and \(d\vec{r} = dx \hat{i}\). \(\vec{F} = (-2x\hat{j})\). \(W_{EF} = \int_{0.5}^{0} 0 dx = 0\) J.
For path FA, \(x=0\) and \(d\vec{r} = dy \hat{j}\). \(\vec{F} = (-y\hat{i})\). \(W_{FA} = \int_{0}^{1} 0 dy = 0\) J.
Total work done in the cycle is the sum of work done in each segment:
W_{total} = W_{AB} + W_{BC} + W_{CD} + W_{DE} + W_{EF} + W_{FA}
W_{total} = -1 + 1 + 0.25 + 0.5 + 0 + 0 = 0.75 J
New work in cycle = 0.75 J
